theater.name: Leader captures and raids
theater.title: Leader captures and raids
theater.sub: A topic tab, not a country: US operations from 1983 to 2026 that captured or killed a country's leader or a top leader of an armed group, cartel or terror group, with the pressure steps around them, and what the target's side did after (attacks, protests, talks).
theater.proxy_note: The target's side is whoever the operation was aimed at: the leader's government, group or cartel, and sometimes the host country. A reply is counted only when the log links it to the US move or it falls inside the window. Statements by blocked state or armed-group media are never cited.
theater.hold_note: Option A has no cases in this tab. There is no single conflict to count quiet weeks in: a week with no US raid against one leader says nothing about another. NAPOR does not invent hold weeks, so the page shows option A as having too few cases.
theater.not_measured: Economic effects (sanctions, trade, prices) are not measured for this tab; that category is left out of the index. Strain with host countries is shown only as logged protests and breaks in relations.
theater.under_logged: The log is a sample of well-documented operations that have a working link in an allowed outlet or official source. Some operations (for example partner captures where no allowed page states the US role) are left out, and most of the rows have not been checked for a reply 30 days after, so "none logged" is not proof nothing happened.

intensity.name: Tension level
intensity.note: Tension level counts logged hostile acts by the target's side (attacks, bombings, missile strikes, hostage-takings; not statements or protests) in the 14 days before each date: 2 points each, +2 if someone died. The log is a sample and the operations are far apart in time and place, so read this as a rough guide only.

econ.text: Not measured. This tab has no clear measure of sanctions, trade or prices across 40 years and many countries, so this category is left out of the index instead of being filled with a made-up number.

people.name: Harm to people
people.other: Share of past cases where anyone was reported hurt in a reply by the target's side within 30 days, or where civilians or others were reported killed or hurt in the US operation itself.
people.hold: Not used: option A has no hold weeks in this tab.

rule.other: Counts when anyone was reported hurt in a reply by the target's side within 30 days of the US move, or when the logged sources report civilians or others killed or hurt in the operation itself.

escalation.name: Escalation
escalation.trigger: Share of past cases followed by a hostile act from the target's side (an attack, a bombing, a missile strike or a hostage-taking) within 30 days.
escalation.other: Share of past cases followed by a hostile act from the target's side within 30 days (timing only).
escalation.hold: Not used: option A has no hold weeks in this tab.

rule.trigger: Counts when the target's side attacked, bombed, fired missiles or took hostages within 30 days (a clear link or timing only). Statements and protests do not count.
rule.other: Counts when the target's side attacked anywhere within 30 days (timing only, not shown to be a reply). Statements and protests do not count.

military.name: Military cost
military.reply: Share of past cases where the reply killed or wounded US troops or destroyed a US aircraft or ship within 30 days.
military.strike: Not used: option A has no hold weeks in this tab.
military.none: No direct military cost is counted for the move itself, so this counts as 0%.

rule.reply: Counts when a reply by the target's side killed or wounded US troops, or destroyed a US aircraft or ship, within 30 days. US losses inside the operation itself are written in the case notes and are not counted here.

economic.name: Economic harm
economic.other: Not measured for this tab. There is no clear measure of sanctions, trade or prices in the log, so this category is shown as "not measured" and left out of the index.
economic.rule: Not measured. Nothing is counted for this category.

political.name: Political / diplomatic
political.other: Share of past cases NOT followed within 14 days by talks (a meeting, a negotiation or a deal) between the US and the target's side or the host government. Protests, statements and breaks in relations do not count as talks.
political.rule: Counts when no talks (a meeting, a negotiation or a deal) between the US and the target's side or the host government were logged within 14 days after the move. Statements, protests and breaks in relations do not count as talks. Rule changed on 2026-10-26.

hostile.title: Air Force history: the US lost 19 killed and about 164 wounded; at least 45 enemy troops were killed and almost 400 wounded (nationalities not split); about 700 Grenadian and Cuban troops were captured and 755 Cubans were sent to Barbados. These losses are the operation itself, so they are a case note for #5001, not a separate reply

TIME (Oct 23, 1989): the coup failed and Giroldi was killed; Noriega jailed 77 opponents and his forces beat scores of others in the streets; US officials said some suspected coup leaders were tortured and executed. Noriega also banned unauthorised assemblies. The crackdown answers the coup itself; no page ties it to the US move

Bush's letter to Congress (Dec 21, 1989): a US Marine officer was killed by Panama Defense Forces personnel on Dec 16 and a US naval officer was beaten and detained and his wife threatened. The letter gives these as reasons for the operation

hostile.actor: Panama Defense Forces and loyalists (target's side)
hostile.title: Fitzwater (Dec 21): 18 US military killed, 117 wounded, 1 missing and 1 civilian dependent killed. The Army's later count is 23 killed and 324 wounded; Panamanian dead are said to be several times the US toll but exact figures are hard to confirm (army.mil). Noriega-controlled radio claimed up to 41 US hostages (CSM, unconfirmed by US officials). CSM (Dec 27): looting began hours after the landing and cost about $1 billion with the bombing. These losses are the operation itself, a case note for #5017

hostile.actor: Somali militia (blamed on Aidid by the UN and US; target's side)
hostile.title: Frontline: 24 Pakistani soldiers were ambushed and killed while inspecting a Somali arms storage site; Clinton's letter and CSM say 23 (counts differ). The UN Security Council condemned the attack in Resolution 837 (Clinton letter). The US and UN blamed Gen. Mohamed Farah Aidid (CSM)
Frontline: four Western journalists are beaten to death by a mob after the Jul 12 helicopter attack

Frontline: a land mine kills four US military police on Aug 8; two weeks later six more US soldiers are wounded in a similar attack. No page read says who planted the mines or ties them to the Jul 12 attack

hostile.actor: Haitian armed crowd and security forces (target's side)
hostile.title: The White House (Oct 12, 1993): the ship arrived at Port-au-Prince when conditions were not secure; the failure of Haitian military and police leaders to protect US personnel was 'a serious obstruction of the Governor's Island process'. The US will press the UN to reimpose sanctions. State Department historian: a mob appeared to threaten violence and the ship pulled away the next day

hostile.actor: Al-Qaeda (target's side; US says bin Laden's network)
hostile.title: Clinton (Aug 20): the bombings killed 12 Americans and nearly 300 Kenyans and Tanzanians and wounded about 5,000; US intelligence attributed them to bin Laden's network. CBS gives 267 dead including 12 Americans

Hundreds of captives claiming to surrender revolt and attack CIA officer Mike Spann, who was interviewing them. CIA calls him the first American killed in combat in Afghanistan. Day 49 after Oct 7: outside the 30-day window of #5300, so it is not linked to it

Hours after the strike on Baghdad Iraq fires missiles at US and British troops in Kuwait; two land in the northern Kuwaiti desert with no chemical material (CNN). Troops masked up and took cover; no casualties confirmed. Iraq's information minister calls the US attack a 'crime against humanity' (NPR)

CNN, Mar 23: US commanders say ten soldiers were killed and 12 missing after Iraqis ambushed a supply convoy that took a wrong turn; Army maintenance unit members were among those captured or killed. Al Jazeera airs Iraqi state TV video of captured and dead US soldiers; Rumsfeld says it violates the Geneva Conventions. At least two Marines killed in combat elsewhere

PBS, Jul 24: three 101st soldiers killed at about 2:30 a.m. near Qayyarah, two days after the raid; two more US soldiers killed in ambushes the day before and another convoy hit a bomb (1 killed, 7 hurt, same page). An Arab satellite channel airs a video of alleged fedayeen vowing revenge: the killings 'will not decrease the attacks against the Americans but rather increase them'. 158 US soldiers killed in action since Mar 20

Al Jazeera: on Sunday, a US occupation soldier was killed while trying to detonate a bomb, CENTCOM confirmed. Bush warned that Saddam's capture would not end attacks on US troops. The page does not say who planted the bomb

NPR: the two soldiers were abducted after a clash in which a third soldier was killed (Friday, Jun 16); their bodies, tortured and booby-trapped, were found late Monday (Jun 19) in Yusufiyah. Al-Qaeda in Iraq claims its new leader 'slaughtered' them (claim unverified). The page does not link the abduction to Zarqawi's death; the group's new leader is the one who replaced him

NBC News: insurgents in stolen UN-marked cars drive into the AU base at Mogadishu airport on Thursday, Sep 17 and blow them up; al-Shabab claims it. At least 16 killed (four were the bombers) and dozens wounded, per witnesses and officials; the AU says nine died at its base, among them a Burundian deputy commander. Missiles fired from the base an hour later killed seven people in insurgent-held areas. At least 30 wounded UN staff were flown out and at least one American was among the wounded (UN personnel, not US forces). NBC says the attackers were 'reportedly' avenging Nabhan, killed on Monday in the US raid; the page gives no direct quote from al-Shabab

hostile.actor: Al-Qaeda in Iraq (target's side; per Iraqi officials)
hostile.title: CSMonitor: coordinated blasts near Moqtada al-Sadr's office during Friday prayers in Sadr City and other bombs in Baghdad kill 54 and hurt 180 overall (Baghdad Operational Command); at least 6 killed in Anbar. Iraqi officials blame al-Qaeda in Iraq and call it retaliation for arrests and the killing of its top leaders. The page does not name the two leaders. Targets were Iraqis, not US forces

NPR: two suicide bombings on Friday kill at least 80 and hurt more than 100, mostly new recruits. The Pakistani Taliban say it was 'to avenge bin Laden's killing'; Pakistani authorities caution that a campaign in Mohmand could also be a motive. Victims were Pakistani, not US

NBC: militants attack the base late Sunday and troops retake it Monday after 16 hours; at least 10 military personnel killed and 20 wounded; a US-supplied Pakistani P-3C Orion destroyed and another aircraft damaged. Spokesman Ehsanullah Ehsan says: 'It was the revenge of martyrdom of Osama bin Laden.' The aircraft belonged to Pakistan, not the US

Gunmen seize Zeidan at dawn from his Tripoli hotel and free him in under six hours. CBS (AP) says it may have been retaliation for the al-Libi raid; a militia anti-crime committee said it was a fraud investigation unrelated to al-Libi, and the prosecutor said no warrant existed. The link to the raid is DISPUTED

hostile.actor: Armed men in Culiacan, Sinaloa (target's side; link to the extradition not established)
hostile.title: Al Jazeera (Mar 15, 2017): a Feb 7 shootout in the Villas del Real neighborhood leaves six dead, five civilians and one marine; the exact circumstances are unclear. The feature describes 'an upsurge in violence following the extradition' of El Chapo: more than 120 murders in Sinaloa in February against a monthly average of 92 over the previous six years. The most repeated explanation is a split inside the Sinaloa cartel, which the author says is hard to verify. Victims were Mexican; no US forces involved

hostile.actor: Iran (per Pentagon and Zarif; also in the Iran tab as #216)
hostile.title: Iran fires more than a dozen ballistic missiles at two Iraqi bases hosting US and coalition troops, about 5:30 p.m. EST Tuesday Jan 7 (early Jan 8 local); Zarif calls it a proportionate measure of self-defense for the base the Soleimani strike came from and says Iran does not seek war. Trump says no Americans were hurt, Iran 'appears to be standing down', and announces new sanctions. Iran's Guard CLAIMED 80 Americans killed, which was not confirmed

hostile.actor: Iran (per PBS, Defense News and ABC; also in the Iran tab as #5)
hostile.title: Iran fires hundreds of missiles and drones at Israel and US bases; Bahrain says its 5th Fleet headquarters was targeted. In week 1 an attack on a base at Port Shuaiba, Kuwait kills six US soldiers. By Mar 28 ABC counts 13 Americans killed (seven in Iranian strikes in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia, six in an aircraft crash in Iraq) and a US official says 300+ troops were hurt. Iran also closes the Strait of Hormuz. Date is the first day

options.what: Take no new step against the leader. This tab has no hold weeks, so option A has no cases here.
risks: No hold weeks are counted for this tab, so there is no hold-week rate. Hostile acts by the target's side are logged at about 0.0 a week in the current phase.

No past cases, so no measure. Strain with host countries: shown only as logged protests.
options.pros: Adds no new US step against a leader, so there is no new US act for the target's side to answer. This tab has no hold weeks, so the log cannot show what happens when the US waits.
options.harms: Leaders stayed in power and kept their groups going. Whether waiting changes what a leader or group does cannot be measured from this log.
options.unknown: No cases. A quiet week for one leader says nothing about another, so NAPOR does not build hold weeks for this tab.

options.name: Negotiate the leader's exit or surrender
options.what: Talk to the leader's side about stepping down, going into exile or surrendering (for example Haiti 1994, Noriega 1988).
risks: No direct casualties from the move itself.
No past cases, so no measure.
No military cost is counted for the move itself.
Economic effects: not measured for this tab. Hostile acts by the target's side are logged at about 0.0 a week in the current phase.
No past cases, so no measure. Strain with host countries: shown only as logged protests.
options.pros: No direct casualties from the talks themselves. In Haiti the junta signed the Carter-Nunn-Powell deal with US troops already in the air (#5037) and Cedras handed over power on Oct 10, 1994 (#5039). Aidid said he would free the captured US pilot a few days after Oakley arrived (#5034, #5035), though Clinton said there was no deal.
options.harms: Talks failed or did not last in several cases: Noriega's talks collapsed at the last minute (#5013), and a crowd at the Port-au-Prince dock turned back a US ship that came to carry out the Governors Island deal (#5033). The Oakley talks came only after the failed Mogadishu raid (#5031). Talking to a leader's side also risks giving it standing.
options.unknown: Few cases, and the talks rows differ a lot (an exile offer, a surrender deal, a UN-backed accord). The Taylor demand of 2003 (#5319) is a demand, not talks. Whether the leader's side saw any offer as a real offer reaches NAPOR only through what was reported.

uses.title: May 17: Reagan says the US is negotiating with Panama but will not discuss it and that the goal is 'a restoration of democracy'. CSM (May 24): the US bypassed Panama's opposition coalition and negotiated privately with Noriega; National Security Adviser Colin Powell indicated the US might drop two indictments if he resigned as defense force commander. CSM (May 20): leaks about dropping the indictments; Vice President Bush said he would never 'bargain' with drug dealers. Logged on the day Reagan confirmed the talks; they had started earlier

The White House (Oct 12, 1993): the Governors Island Agreement was signed Jul 3, 1993 after US negotiations with the UN and OAS; it brought a new government under Prime Minister Malval and an amnesty. The State Department historian: it called for President Aristide's return by Oct 30, 1993. AP (1994): Cedras had broken earlier promises to leave

AP via CSM (Oct 12): Clinton's envoy Oakley arrives in Mogadishu to seek a diplomatic end to the fighting; Aideed reportedly ordered his men to stop fighting and said he would accept an independent inquiry into the Jun 5 ambush; thousands of Somalis protested against the UN and US that day. Clinton (Oct 14): 'no deal' for Durant; the US wants the arrest warrant honoured but 'there may be other ways'

Clinton announces that Haiti's military leaders will step down once parliament passes an amnesty law, and no later than Oct 15; US-led troops arrive from Sep 19 under UN Security Council Resolution 940. AP: 61 planes with 82nd Airborne paratroopers were already in the air and were recalled. CSM (Sep 20): de facto president Emile Jonassaint signed after 32 hours of talks with the US delegation; the text does not require the leaders to leave Haiti

Al Jazeera, Aug 10: Taylor, due to step down on Monday under international pressure, says 'This is an American war', calls the rebel LURD a 'surrogate force', tells the US to 'call off their dogs' and says he is being pushed into exile (Nigeria most likely). The page says Bush told Taylor to step down and does not mention US troops. No US-Taylor talks are logged

options.name: Indict, offer a reward or sanction the leader
options.what: Legal and money pressure on a named leader: an indictment, a reward, or sanctions on that person (for example Noriega, bin Laden, Maduro).
risks: No direct casualties from sanctions or a reward on a leader. Harm to ordinary people from sanctions: not measured.
No past cases, so no measure.
No military cost is counted for the move itself.
Economic effects: not measured for this tab. Hostile acts by the target's side are logged at about 0.0 a week in the current phase.
No past cases, so no measure. Strain with host countries: shown only as logged protests.
options.pros: Legal and money pressure with no direct casualties and no risk to US forces: the Noriega indictment (#5011), the bin Laden executive order and indictment (#5043, #5046), and rewards or indictments for Saddam, Zarqawi, Baghdadi and Maduro (#5316, #5323, #5609, #5620, #5631).
options.harms: Pressure did not remove the leader on its own in these cases. Noriega stayed until the 1989 invasion (#5017), and the Taliban answered the bin Laden indictment by refusing to hand him over (#5047). Harm to ordinary people from sanctions is not measured.
options.unknown: Rewards and indictments rarely have a dated reply. Most rows have not been checked for a reply 30 days after, and the log has only the best-documented rounds, not every reward or sanction.

uses.title: On Feb 4, 1988 a federal grand jury indicts Noriega on drug-related charges (11th Circuit opinion). TIME (1992): the indictment came while he was still ruling Panama. The Bush letter to Congress (Dec 21, 1989) calls it the '1988 indictment'. The Tampa grand jury is not confirmed in the pages read

Frontline: Admiral Howe orders Aidid's arrest and offers a $25,000 reward (the page's date for it is inferred). CSM (Jun 21) and Clinton's Jul 1 letter confirm the UN arrest order; Clinton's Oct 14 news conference mentions 'the $25,000 bounty'. An order of the UN envoy, not the US government

Executive Order 13099, signed Aug 20 and in force from 12:01 a.m. Aug 21, adds four names to the Annex of E.O. 12947: bin Laden, the Islamic Army (al-Qaida), Abu Hafs al-Masri and Rifa'i Ahmad Taha Musa. CSM (Aug 24): Clinton banned financial transactions between US companies and bin Laden

A Manhattan federal court indicts bin Laden and al-Qaeda military commander Muhammad Atef over the Aug 7 embassy bombings; the State Department announces rewards of up to $5 million each (USIA text; CBS). CBS: investigators did not expect to capture bin Laden soon because he was protected by allies in Afghanistan

FBI Director Freeh announces bin Laden as the 456th name on the list, citing the Nov 4, 1998 indictment for the embassy bombings; the State Department's Diplomatic Security Service offers up to $5 million, the largest reward ever offered for a US fugitive (USIA text). CBS (AP): he replaced the Lockerbie suspects after Libya agreed to hand them over; the FBI also tied him to the 1996 Saudi barracks bombing

The US occupation authority offers $25 million for information leading to the capture or confirmed death of Saddam Hussein and $15 million for each of his sons; Bremer urges people with information to come forward (Al Jazeera)

Secretary of State Powell authorises raising the reward for al-Zarqawi from $10 million to $25 million (Al Jazeera, Jul 1). CBS (Oct 30, 2003) said the State Department had first posted $25 million and revised it down to $5 million, which does not match the $10 million 'before' figure here

The State Department raises the reward for ISIS leader Baghdadi from $10 million (set in 2011) to $25 million, the top tier; the US says the threat from him has 'increased significantly' since 2011. The page read is dated Dec 17, 2016 and links a Dec 16 Washington Post report, so Dec 16 is an inference

Attorney General Barr announces narco-terrorism and drug-smuggling charges against Maduro and other leaders; the State Department offers $15 million for Maduro's capture. NPR gives 'Thursday'; Mar 26 comes from the page URL. The page does not report Venezuela's reaction
Attorney General Bondi announces in a video that the reward for Maduro is doubled to $50 million and says the Justice Department has seized more than $700 million in assets linked to him

options.name: Capture raid
options.what: Special forces or law enforcement take the person alive (for example Saddam Hussein 2003, Abu Anas al-Libi 2013, Maduro 2026). Failed or partial raids are counted and flagged.

cases.actor: US (Delta Force, per a US military official)
cases.title: US special forces seize Nazih Abdul-Hamed al-Ruqai, known as Abu Anas al-Libi, outside his home after dawn prayers; he was indicted in New York over the 1998 East Africa embassy bombings and carried a $5 million bounty. He is taken to a secure location outside Libya; the Pentagon says he is 'lawfully detained under the law of war'. Libya says it was not told in advance. Captured alive. The same morning's Somalia raid failed (#5601)

PM Zeidan says Libya 'would not surrender its sons' but wants to keep good ties. Secretary of State Kerry calls al-Libi a 'legal and appropriate target'. Date is the Monday the ambassador was summoned (NPR)

cases.actor: US (special forces and air operation 'Absolute Resolve'; also in the Venezuela tab as #4049)
cases.title: More than 150 aircraft and low-flying helicopters take part in an overnight raid on Maduro's compound; US forces are on the ground from about 1:01 to 3:29 a.m. EST; Maduro and his wife are flown to a US warship and then to New York, where a Justice Department indictment was released. One helicopter was hit by fire but flew safely home. Delcy Rodriguez says Venezuelan civilians and military were killed; no total on the page read. Trump says the US will 'run' the country until a new leader is chosen. Captured alive
cases.note: Maduro seized Jan 3, 2026. Searched Jan 3-24 with Al Jazeera (Jan 6 and Jan 24 pages): no hostile act by Venezuela's side, no attack on US forces or Americans, no street protests and no break in relations (the government is described as biting its tongue). Not hostile acts: Rodriguez called it a 'kidnapping' (Jan 4-6), the UN Security Council condemned it, 47 Venezuelan military were honored at a Jan 22 vigil. Talks: Rodriguez invited US cooperation Jan 4; a US-Venezuela oil export plan was announced days after Jan 3, the CIA director went to Caracas and Trump and Rodriguez spoke by phone (a linked headline dates the call Jan 15; the dates in the page text are missing). Jan 25-Feb 2 was not searched.
cases.dmg: A few US personnel injured, none killed (Trump); one helicopter hit; Venezuelan civilians and military killed (Rodriguez, no total)

risks: Replies that hurt people: 1 of 3 logged: #5322 1 US soldier killed. People reported hurt in the US operation itself are shown on each case.
The target's side attacked, bombed or took hostages within 30 days: 2 of 3 (67%) (range 21%-94%). Fast (within 2 days): 2 of 3. Back-and-forth past one reply: ~7% (all chains, n=28).

US troops were killed or wounded, or a US aircraft or ship was lost, in a reply within 30 days in 1 of 3 past cases. Losses inside the operation itself are written in the case notes and are not counted.
Economic effects (sanctions, trade, prices): not measured for this tab. This category is left out of the index.
Talks (a meeting, a negotiation or a deal) within 14 days after: 0 of 3 (protests, statements and breaks in relations do not count). Strain with host countries: shown only as logged protests.
options.pros: The person is taken alive, which keeps the chance of a trial: Saddam Hussein (#5321), Abu Anas al-Libi (#5600), Ahmed Abu Khattala (#5604), Mustafa al-Imam (#5612) and Maduro (#5633). In most of these the sources report no US deaths in the raid itself.
options.harms: Raids can fail and can cost lives: the Mogadishu raid of Oct 3-4, 1993 left 18 US dead (#5031) and the Somalia capture attempt of Oct 2013 failed (#5601). After the al-Libi raid Libya summoned the US ambassador and gunmen briefly held its prime minister (#5602, #5603), and Libya protested the Khattala raid as an attack on its sovereignty (#5605). A US soldier was killed by a bomb the day after Saddam's capture (#5322); the page does not say who planted it.
options.unknown: Few cases, spread over 40 years and very different places. Most rows have not been checked for a reply 30 days after. The Maduro capture (#5633) is also in the Venezuela tab, and what followed there is logged in that tab.

uses.title: At the President's direction US F-14s from the carrier Saratoga find the aircraft and escort it to the Sigonella air base in Italy without firing a shot (White House statement). It lands with Italian consent and the hijackers go into Italian custody. CSM: the plane had left Egypt carrying the hijackers, Egyptian officials and two PLO leaders. The US later named PLF leader Muhammad Abbas as the mastermind (#5006). Partial capture: the hijackers were held, the leader was not

CSM (Oct 18): the Oct 3-4 firefight with forces loyal to Aideed cost 18 US troops, a Malaysian soldier and two US helicopters. Failed capture raid: the aim was to seize Aidid's circle and the hunt for him was abandoned on Oct 7 (#5032). The raid's named targets are not in the pages read

The White House says he will not go to Guantanamo. NPR gives only 'Sunday'; Al Jazeera gives Jun 15. Captured alive

ABC says only 'this weekend'; the Oct 29 date and the Misurata area come from NBC's court story. Captured alive

uses.title: President Reagan tells Congress that about 1,900 US Army and Marine personnel began landing in Grenada, with about 300 from the OECS states, Jamaica and Barbados. He cites up to 1,000 US citizens on the island, the killing of Bishop and others ('over 40 killings') and no working government. The Air Force history dates the operation Oct 24 - Nov 3, 1983. The ruling military council is not named in the pages read

Bush's memo of Dec 20 authorises US forces to arrest Noriega and others under US drug indictments and hand them to US law enforcement. Fitzwater lists four aims: protect American lives, support democracy, bring Noriega to justice, protect the canal treaties. The operation began at 1 a.m.; about 11,000 more US forces joined about 13,000 already there (letter to Congress). CSM: air and artillery fire, tanks and paratroopers; Guillermo Endara sworn in as president about an hour before; Powell said organised resistance ended about seven hours in. Noriega was not found that day

President Bush: Noriega turned himself in to US authorities in Panama at about 8:50 p.m. with the Panamanian government's knowledge, was taken to Howard Air Force Base where the DEA arrested him, and was flown to Homestead Air Force Base in Florida to be arraigned in Miami. Army.mil: he had spent 10 days in the Vatican embassy while US forces played rock music outside. The first US combat troops had already left Panama

CSM (Sep 20): US forces landed on Monday morning, the second US occupation of Haiti this century, with the cooperation of the Haitian military; first targets were the Port-au-Prince airport and seaport. The planned force was about 15,000 troops (Clinton). The same page reports gunfire in the streets and fear of sniper fire. Aristide returned Oct 15 (State Department historian)

At 1 p.m. ET President Bush says the US military has begun strikes against al-Qaeda training camps in Afghanistan (NPR); the White House page for the address describes the targets as al-Qaeda camps and Taliban military sites. US air attacks drove the Taliban from most of their territory and Kandahar was reported surrendered on Dec 7 (AP, #5304). Bin Laden and Mullah Omar had not been captured by then

uses.title: Attorney General Reno: Mexican authorities arrested Garcia Abrego on the evening of Jan 14 and expelled him the next day; he was taken into federal custody in Houston on Jan 15. A 1993 Texas indictment accuses him of leading a Mexican organisation that moved tons of cocaine for the Cali cartel; he had been on the FBI Ten Most Wanted list since Mar 1995. CSM (Jan 17): arrested near Monterrey; a $2 million reward had been announced; a US-born citizen

Mexico extradites El Chapo to the US on Obama's last full day in office; he is flown to Long Island MacArthur airport, New York and faces drug-trafficking charges. The page reports no violence tied to the extradition and no Mexican reaction

Honduras extradites its former president; he is brought to New York. He is charged with conspiring to import cocaine and with machine-gun and destructive-device counts; he was arrested in Tegucigalpa in February and Honduras' Supreme Court upheld the extradition in March. DEA's administrator calls it a warning to leaders who help transnational crime

Mexico extradites Ovidio Guzman, captured by Mexican forces on Jan 5, 2023; he is flown to Chicago and also faces charges in New York and Washington. Attorney General Garland credits 'US and Mexico law enforcement cooperation'. The page recalls that gunmen flooded Culiacan in 2019 when he was briefly detained

Zambada boards a plane with Joaquin Guzman Lopez, who was helping US investigators, thinking they were inspecting property in Mexico; it lands near El Paso and FBI agents arrest both men. Mexican officials say the US embassy told them and that Mexico did not take part in the detention or surrender. Letter H is the closest fit but this is neither an extradition nor a raid

Mexico flies 29 prisoners from an airport north of Mexico City to eight US cities, its largest handover in years, days before 25% US tariffs were due; Attorney General Bondi confirms the US has them. Mexico calls it a 'transfer' and it is unclear whether a formal extradition process was used. The page reports no violence afterward
